paragraphs.heading: What an amine is
paragraphs.text: Amines are organic compounds that contain bonds between carbon and nitrogen. You can picture one as ammonia in which one or more hydrogen atoms have been swapped for alkyl or aryl groups. The nitrogen atom in an amine carries a lone pair of electrons.

paragraphs.heading: Three classes
paragraphs.text: Amines come in three classes, set by how many groups sit on the nitrogen. A primary amine has one alkyl or aryl group, with the general formula RNH₂, and its −NH₂ part is called the amino group. A secondary amine has two such groups, R₂NH, and a tertiary amine has three, R₃N.

paragraphs.heading: Familiar examples
paragraphs.text: Methylamine, most amino acids and the buffering agent tris are important primary amines. Aniline, C₆H₇N, a benzene ring joined to an amino group, is the simplest aromatic amine. Dimethylamine is a secondary amine, and trimethylamine, a tertiary amine, has a distinctly fishy smell. Amines can also form rings, such as the three-membered aziridine and the six-membered piperidine, and these cyclic amines are either secondary or tertiary.

paragraphs.heading: Close relatives
paragraphs.text: Two related kinds of compound go by other names. If the nitrogen is attached to a carbonyl group, giving R−C(=O)−NR′R″, the compound is an amide. If the nitrogen carries four organic groups, giving R₄N⁺X⁻, the compound is a quaternary ammonium salt.

paragraphs.heading: Hydrogen bonds and smell
paragraphs.text: Hydrogen bonding strongly shapes how primary and secondary amines behave. Methyl and ethyl amines are gases at standard conditions, while methyl and ethyl alcohols are liquids. Hydrogen bonding through the lone pair also helps simple amines dissolve in water. Amines smell like ammonia, and the liquid ones have a foul, fishy odor.

paragraphs.heading: Grabbing a hydrogen ion
paragraphs.text: The lone pair on nitrogen can bind a hydrogen ion, H⁺, turning the amine into an ammonium ion, R₃NH⁺. In aromatic amines such as aniline, the lone pair is shared out into the benzene ring, so these amines form hydrogen bonds less readily. They have high boiling points and dissolve poorly in water.

paragraphs.heading: Spotting an amine
paragraphs.text: Chemists usually confirm an amine by combining mass spectrometry with NMR and IR spectroscopy. The ¹H NMR signals of an amine vanish when the sample is treated with D₂O. In an infrared spectrum, primary and secondary amines show N–H stretching bands near 3300 cm⁻¹. A primary amine gives two of these N–H bands, while a secondary amine gives only one.
